column4: The people are presented before their Lord in one row, صَفًّا; this is the human counterpart to the section’s repeated rows of arriving angels.

The Spirit and angels stand صَفًّا on the Day of Judgment. Their fixed assembly extends the section’s image from arrival to the ordered gathering, under the verse’s rule that speech requires permission.

The angels say they are الصَّافُّونَ, “those in ranks,” directly naming the arrangement in the section. The preceding 37:164 adds that each has a known station, clarifying the standing-place sense of the section’s dictionary form المَصَفّ.
The oath by الصَّافَّاتِ صَفًّا invokes beings arranged in ranks; it supplies another explicit image of the ordered formation named in the section.

Here the singular collective الْمَلَكُ stands at the sky’s edges as it splits, matching the section’s note that الْمَلَكُ can name the whole angelic class and placing the rows in a larger judgment scene.

The verse asks whether people await God’s coming in canopies of cloud with the angels, a specific expected arrival matching the section’s scene; it then warns that the matter will be decided and returned to God.

This warning asks whether people await the angels, their Lord, or signs of their Lord to come. It voices the same awaited arrival while its own context stresses that belief after the signs appear will not benefit a soul.
On the day the sky splits with clouds, angels are sent down in a descent. Their arrival continues the section’s end-time scene, though this verse does not say they stand in rows.
Prophets and witnesses are brought, وَجِيءَ بِالنَّبِيِّينَ وَالشُّهَدَاءِ, for judgment; this is a concrete instance of the section’s dictionary sense of bringing something into presence.
Every soul comes accompanied by a driver and a witness, سَائِقٌ وَشَهِيدٌ. This gives the section’s general arrival a personal form, with each person escorted and attested.
Hell is exposed to whoever sees it, وَبُرِّزَتِ الْجَحِيمُ لِمَن يَرَىٰ. This specifies the section’s bringing of Hell as a disclosure into sight.
Hell is exposed to the misguided, وَبُرِّزَتِ الْجَحِيمُ لِلْغَاوِينَ; its own context identifies who faces the revelation that the section depicts.
Hell is displayed to the disbelievers on that day. Its being set before them parallels the section’s brought-forward Hell, while 18:99 supplies the preceding trumpet and gathering.
Disbelievers are driven to Hell in groups, زُمَرًا: the section brings Hell to the scene, while this verse reverses the direction and brings the people to it.
The God-fearing are likewise led in groups to the Garden; this same judgment procession shows the other destination alongside the section’s brought-forward Hell.
Paradise is brought near to the God-fearing, a favorable counterpart to the section’s Hell brought into view; the verse makes the opposed destinations visible in the same judgment setting.

The section’s dictionary form تَتْرَى means “one after another”; here messengers are sent in succession, and each community’s denial is followed by the next until they become tales. This makes the section’s repeated sequence concrete.

The earth and mountains are carried and crushed with one crushing, فَدُكَّتَا دَكَّةً وَاحِدَةً. This directly parallels the section’s dictionary root د ك ك for pounding the ground before the rows arrive.

The mountains are blown away and the land left a level plain, قَاعًا صَفْصَفًا; 20:107 completes the picture by saying there is no crookedness or elevation on it. It gives the flattened stage preceding the section’s rows.
The mountains are moved, the earth is seen bare, and all are gathered; 18:48 then presents them before their Lord in a row. This links the cleared ground to the human formation that follows.
The earth is violently shaken; 56:5–6 continue with mountains crumbling into scattered dust. This is another explicit earth-breaking scene beside the section’s pounding of the ground.

The earth is shaken with its great earthquake, and 99:2 continues by having it cast out its burdens. The sequence gives the section’s ground-pounding a parallel in the upheaval before the earth’s final disclosure.
The earth is stretched out and empties what is within it in 84:4; this is a related preparation of the final ground, though stretching and emptying are not the section’s pounding or rows.

Each angel says it has a known station, مَقَامٌ مَعْلُومٌ; the next verse, 37:165, identifies them as standing in ranks. The row’s own station detail develops the section’s dictionary form المَصَفّ, “standing-place.”
Believers fighting in God’s cause are loved when they stand in a row, صَفًّا, like a solid structure. This gives the section’s straight-line formation a specific earthly counterpart.

Moses’ opponents are told to come صفًّا, in line, for the contest. The same physical formation stages a human confrontation, a boundary showing that a row by itself does not mean the section’s final assembly.

At Badr God promises a thousand angels “following one another,” مُرْدِفِينَ. Their successive arrival parallels the section’s repeated ranks, while this verse places it in a battle rather than the final gathering.
At the trumpet, people emerge from their graves hastening to their Lord. This is another collective movement toward the Lord, though the verse pictures haste rather than the section’s ordered rows.
A single blast brings everyone before God; 36:51 gives the preceding emergence from graves. This provides a compact parallel to the section’s arrival and presentation scene.
When the trumpet is blown, people come in groups, أَفْوَاجًا. It parallels the section’s repeated arrival, but groups are not the straight, repeated lines described there.

People hasten toward the Caller, and 54:7 pictures them emerging from graves like scattered locusts. This is a judgment crowd moving toward a summons, with a dispersed form that contrasts with the section’s rows.
People rush from their graves toward a caller like scattered locusts; this is a specific mass-arrival scene whose scattering contrasts with the section’s ordered lines.
On that day people are like scattered moths. This same judgment crowd is pictured as dispersed, a concrete visual boundary to the section’s rows.

Angels encircle the Throne at the judgment’s conclusion, praising God as judgment is passed. This places an angelic assembly in the same final scene, though its circular arrangement differs from the section’s rows.
The sky is split open on that day, and 69:17 places the angels at its edges. The cited verse’s torn sky is the setting that completes the section’s arrival scene.
A single trumpet blast begins the sequence in which 69:14 says earth and mountains are crushed together; it supplies the event’s onset before the section’s flattened ground and rows.
The earth and mountains shake, and the mountains become heaps of moving sand. This is a specific companion image of the final earth’s upheaval, though it does not itself show the rows.
The earth splits from the dead and they emerge rapidly; gathering them is described as easy for God. This gives the section’s incoming assembly another explicit emergence toward divine judgment.

This passage names Thamud and ʿĀd as denying the overwhelming event; 69:5–10 then recount their destruction and other punished peoples. It echoes the section’s sequence of past communities before its final scene.

Thamud are destroyed by the overwhelming calamity; 69:4 names them with ʿĀd, and 69:6–10 extend the chain of punished peoples. This connects the section’s named sequence with another account of successive judgment.
ʿĀd are struck by a furious wind, followed in 69:7 by seven nights and eight days of it; the account continues the sequence of earlier punished peoples recalled in the section.

The wind against ʿĀd continues for seven nights and eight days, حُسُومًا; 69:8 asks whether any remnant remains. Its consecutive duration echoes the section’s interest in what comes one after another, within a specific destruction narrative.
After the preceding wind against ʿĀd, the verse asks whether any remnant can be seen. This supplies the aftermath of the successive communal destructions recalled in the section.
Pharaoh, those before him, and the overturned cities are named as further communities in error; 69:10 gives their seizure. The list parallels the section’s sequence that includes Pharaoh.
They disobey their Lord’s messenger and are seized; 69:9 names Pharaoh and the overturned cities. This gives the punishment behind the sequence of communities recalled in the section.

The section’s secondary dictionary form of ف ج ر describes calamities bursting over a people; here فَانفَجَرَتْ is a spring bursting from a struck rock into twelve water sources. The shared root makes a concrete life-giving counter-sense to the section’s disaster image.

After the barrier opens, people surge over one another, يَمُوجُ فِي بَعْضٍ, as the trumpet is blown and all are gathered. This is the section’s dictionary root د ك ك crowding image in a final-day scene, with chaotic waves as a contrast to ordered rows; 18:100 then displays Hell.

People follow the Caller on that Day with no deviation, and their voices are humbled; 20:107 describes the level plain they cross. The verse adds directed, orderly movement toward a summons beside the section’s arrival in rows.

The criminals see the Fire and know they are about to fall into it, finding no escape. This gives the section’s exposed Hell a specific human response: recognition that its appearance means their unavoidable destination.
Each person will come to the Merciful on Resurrection Day alone, فَرْدًا. This individual arrival is a specific counter-image to the section’s collective rows of angels.

On the day each soul comes pleading for itself and is repaid for what it did, arrival leads directly to personal accounting. It complements the section’s arrival scene with what that encounter requires of each person.

The earth and heavens are replaced, and all come before God, the One, the Irresistible. This joins the section’s transformed ground to the arrival before the Lord, while depicting a cosmic remaking rather than a flattened surface.

When wrongdoers see the angels, the verse says there is no good news for them that day; 25:25 continues with the sky splitting and angels descending. It supplies the fearful human side of the angelic appearance in the section.

Gog and Magog are released and rush down from every elevation; this gives the section’s dictionary sense of د ك ك as a crowd surging over something a distinct end-time mass movement, chaotic rather than in ranks.
This list names Noah’s people, ʿĀd, and Pharaoh before the next verse names Thamud and other factions. Its own contribution is to repeat the section’s sequence of named earlier communities.
Thamud, Lot’s people, and the dwellers of the thicket continue the preceding list of earlier factions in 38:12; Thamud directly overlaps the section’s succession of punished peoples.

The verse lists ʿĀd, Thamud, the people of al-Rass, and many generations between them. This is another explicit chain of communities like the section’s remembered sequence of ʿĀd, Thamud, and Pharaoh.

The people of Noah, the companions of al-Rass, and Thamud are named as earlier deniers; 50:13 continues the chain with ʿĀd and Pharaoh. Its own list repeats two peoples in the section’s historical sequence.

This verse names ʿĀd, Pharaoh, and Lot’s people among those before; 50:12 precedes it with Noah’s people and Thamud, and 50:14 concludes that these groups denied messengers and the threat came true. It repeats the section’s succession of former peoples.

The verse says the people of the thicket and Tubbaʿ denied the messengers, so the threat came true; 50:12–13 supply the preceding series, including Thamud, ʿĀd, and Pharaoh. It completes a parallel chain of rejected communities and judgment.

The section’s secondary dictionary form of ف ج ر describes calamities bursting over a people; here opponents demand that a spring be made to burst from the earth. This is a concrete counter-sense of the root, continued by the demand for rivers in 17:91.
The demand is for rivers to gush through a garden, using the section’s root ف ج ر in a provision scene rather than its dictionary image of sudden calamity; 17:90 gives the preceding spring demand.

When the command comes, the town is overturned and stones rain down on it. This is a specific sudden, cascading punishment of a people like the section’s secondary dictionary image of disasters bursting upon them.
The town is overturned and stones of baked clay rain down upon its people. This repeats the sudden destructive onslaught described in the section’s secondary dictionary sense of ف ج ر.

The people of Lot are rained upon, and the verse calls it a rain for the criminals. This is another concrete cascading punishment of a community alongside the section’s dictionary image of calamities bursting upon people.
A rain is poured on Lot’s people and described as a terrible rain for those warned. This repeats the section’s specific image of sudden calamity descending on a people.
